sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.summary: FHWA-SA-02-054 consolidates four decades of shallow foundation research and practice for transportation professionals responsible for design, procurement, and construction of shallow foundations for bridges and other transportation structures. Draws from FHWA, SHA, and published guidance. Special emphasis on abutments on compacted approach fills.
sections.body: (p. 1) This Geotechnical Engineering Circular (GEC) coalesces more than four decades of research, development and practical experience in the application of shallow foundations for support of transportation structures. The document is intended to be a definitive desk reference for the transportation professional responsible for design, procurement and construction of shallow foundations for bridges and other transportation-related structures. This GEC draws heavily from previous published work by FHWA, State (and Local) Highway Agencies (SHAs) and other authors of practical guidance related to shallow foundations. It is intended to provide a single reference source for state-of-the-practice information on the design and construction of shallow foundations. Special attention has been given to case histories and design examples on the use of shallow foundations to support abutments in compacted approach embankments.
key_points: Consolidates four decades of research and practice for shallow foundation design
Intended as a definitive desk reference for transportation professionals
Draws from FHWA, SHA, and other published guidance sources
Provides state-of-the-practice information as a single reference source
Special emphasis on shallow foundations bearing on compacted structural fills
Includes case histories for abutments supported in compacted approach embankments
sections.applicability: Design, procurement, and construction of shallow foundations for bridges and transportation-related structures.

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Shallow foundations are usually the most cost-effective support; bridges often use piles from past (railroad) practice. Piles are wise, if not essential, for scour, poor ground, vessel impact, seismicity and congested urban sites. Studies: about 600,000 U.S. bridges at about $500,000 each, half in the substructure; shallow foundations cost 50-65% of deep (Briaud & Gibbens 1995); WSDOT built 500+ bridges on spread footings 1965-1980; FHWA's 21 bridges: 70% of settlement before the deck, post-deck average under 6 mm (1/4 in.).
sections.body: (pp. 1-3) Shallow foundations are the simplest form of load transfer to the ground: small excavations, no specialized equipment, relatively inexpensive, and in most cases the most cost-effective choice. Bridges are nevertheless frequently supported on driven piles, perhaps as much from continued past practice as anything else, rooted in railroad practice, where constant grades over varied ground made piles the obvious choice before soil mechanics existed; early highway engineers were largely ex-rail engineers. Pile support is often wise, if not essential: waterway crossings need protection from scour and other water hazards; poor ground and transient loads such as vessel impact or seismicity may dictate deep foundations; and in congested urban and suburban sites a small-footprint deep foundation may cost less than shoring, utility relocation and right-of-way for a shallow one. But many bridges are at upland developments and interchanges, away from waterways and on competent ground, and engineers should look for prudent, cost-effective use of shallow foundations there. Competent ground plus good-quality granular fill is an opportunity: abutments supported within compacted approach fills save through a shorter schedule, deleting piles through the fill to competent material, and less concrete and steel where a footing was detailed below the fill. Studies: about 600,000 highway bridges in the U.S., average replacement cost about $500,000, about 50 percent of it the substructure; shallow foundations can generally be built for 50 to 65 percent of the cost of deep foundations (Briaud & Gibbens, 1995); WSDOT built more than 500 bridges between 1965 and 1980 with one or more abutments or piers on spread footings (DiMillio, 1982) and still uses footings in structural fills regularly; in 1986 FHWA evaluated 21 bridge foundations on shallow foundations on cohesionless soil: 70 percent of settlement occurred before the deck was placed and the average post-deck settlement was less than 6 mm (1/4 inch) (Gifford et al., 1987). Conclusions: sufficient financial incentive exists to use shallow foundations where feasible; they have a proven track record on hundreds of bridge projects; and sufficient performance data exist to alleviate settlement concerns where good ground exists.
key_points: Shallow foundations are the simplest and, in most cases, the most cost-effective load transfer
Piles on bridges may be as much from past (railroad) practice as from any other reason
Piles are wise, if not essential, for scour, poor ground, vessel impact or seismicity, and congested urban sites
About 600,000 U.S. highway bridges at about $500,000 replacement each; about 50% is substructure
Shallow foundations generally cost 50-65% of deep foundations (Briaud & Gibbens, 1995)
WSDOT built 500+ bridges on spread footings between 1965 and 1980 (DiMillio, 1982)
FHWA (1986), 21 bridges on cohesionless soil: 70% of settlement before deck placement; post-deck average under 6 mm (1/4 in.) (Gifford et al., 1987)
Upland sites with competent ground and good granular fill are opportunities for abutments in compacted approach fills
sections.applicability: Evaluation of whether shallow foundations are appropriate versus deep foundations for bridge and transportation structures, particularly at sites with competent ground conditions.

sections.title: Relevant Publications
sections.summary: Supplementary publications: AASHTO Standard Specifications (16th Ed., 1996), AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specs (2nd Ed., 1998), NHI 132037 Shallow Foundations Workshop Manual (Munfakh et al. 2000), NHI 13212 Soils and Foundations (Cheney & Chassie 2000), NHI 132031 Subsurface Investigation (Arman et al. 1997), Foundation Engineering Handbook (Fang 1991).
sections.body: (p. 3) Although the Shallow Foundations GEC is intended to be a stand-alone reference document, additional detail and background on the methods and procedures can be found in the following publications: AASHTO Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges, 16th Edition, with 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000 Interim Revisions (AASHTO, 1996); AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, 2nd Edition, with 1999, 2000 and 2001 Interim Revisions (AASHTO, 1998); NHI 13212 Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000); NHI 132037 Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Munfakh et al., 2000); NHI 132031 Subsurface Investigation Workshop Reference Manual (Arman et al., 1997); NHI 132035 Module 5 - Rock Slopes: Design, Excavation and Stabilization (Wyllie & Mah, 1998); Foundation Engineering Handbook (Fang, 1991); Soil Mechanics (Lambe & Whitman, 1969); Rock Slope Engineering (Hoek & Bray, 1981).
key_points: GEC is designed as a stand-alone reference but supplements other key publications
AASHTO Standard Specifications (16th Ed.) and LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2nd Ed.) are primary design codes
NHI 132037 is the companion Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual
NHI 13212 covers general soils and foundations; NHI 132031 covers subsurface investigation
Rock slope references (NHI 132035, Hoek & Bray 1981) provide guidance for foundations on rock
sections.applicability: Reference list for practitioners needing additional detail beyond this GEC on shallow foundation design methods and subsurface investigation.

sections.title: Shallow Foundation Systems Applications
sections.summary: Shallow foundations distribute structural loads over large near-surface areas. Highway applications include bridge abutments on slopes or embankments, intermediate piers, retaining walls, culverts, sign posts, noise barriers, rest stop and maintenance building foundations, and mat or footing support for column loads. Suitable subsurface conditions must be confirmed.
sections.body: (p. 4) Shallow foundations principally distribute structural loads over large areas of near-surface soil or rock to lower the intensity of the applied loads to levels tolerable for the foundation soils. Shallow foundations are used in many applications in highway projects when the subsurface conditions are appropriate. Such applications include bridge abutments on soil slopes or embankments, bridge intermediate piers, retaining walls, culverts, sign posts, noise barriers, and rest stop or maintenance building foundations. Footings or mats may support column loads under buildings. Bridge piers are often supported on shallow foundations using various structural configurations.
key_points: Shallow foundations distribute loads over large areas to reduce bearing stress intensity
Applications include bridge abutments, intermediate piers, retaining walls, culverts, sign posts, and noise barriers
Also used for rest stop and maintenance building foundations
Footings or mats may support column loads under buildings
Subsurface conditions must be appropriate for shallow foundation use
sections.applicability: All highway project applications where near-surface soil or rock conditions can support structural loads at tolerable stress levels.
